newsitem.title: USA: Hemingway name a money-spinner in Florida.
newsitem.headline: Hemingway name a money-spinner in Florida.

text.p: The Ernest Hemingway name has drawn thousands of tourists and millions of dollars to this Florida Keys island over the years, and residents like to see his image staring back from racks of T-shirts.
Business people say Hemingway's legacy belongs to Key West and they have no plans to drop him from their marketing efforts, although Hemingway's sons want them to stop.

"Hemingway lived here for 10 years. Are we really going to erase that decade from 1930 to 1940," said Michael Walton, organiser of the annual Hemingway Days festival which has been held in Key West every July since 1981.

Walton said this week he had been forced to cancel the 10-day fiesta of literary seminars, writing competitions, drinking and arm wrestling contests because of a threat of a law suit from Hemingway's three sons.
Patrick Hemingway said from his home in Bozeman, Montana, that the festival portrayed his father as "a slob." He said he wanted to stop it before the centennial of his birth in 1899.

The sons also wanted a share of the profits. A letter to Whalton demanded 10 percent of the income and back payments for the past five years. They demanded control of the event and use of the Hemingway name.

But Key West has long made the most of the Hemingway legacy. His former house on Whitehead Street is a huge tourist draw and at least two bars have capitalised on their connection with one of the century's most celebrated drinkers.

Hemingway lived in Key West from 1929 to 1940, fishing, carousing and writing such works as "Death in the Afternoon" and "The Snows of Kilimanjaro." The novel "To Have and Have Not" is set in Key West.
Paintings and photographs of him are sold in more than a dozen stores in Duvall Street, where the Nobel laureate once strolled with the day's catch.
More than 200,000 tourists a year pay $6.50 to tour the author's former home. Jewelry store owner Mary Dickson bought the Hemingway House from the family in 1961 after his death.
Today the tourism proceeds go to a private corporation owned by Dickson's heirs. She died in 1989.
Patrick Hemingway said the display, which includes a studio where the author supposedly wrote several novels, is a sham. "There's not a single authentic object in the Hemingway House," he said.

Patrick, who lived there in the 1930s while attending school, said the story behind the 60 cats that live there was also a lie. According to tour guides, they are relatives of a cat given to Hemingway by a ship's captain for good luck.
Michael Morawski, the house's manager, said the exhibit was a living memorial to the author complete with orginal furniture that was found in a storage shed in Key West.

At Sloppy Joe's on Duvall Street, customers pass by a souvenir shop selling T-shirts, beer mugs and baseball caps emblazoned with the man's visage before reaching the bar, once Hemingway's favourite haunt.

The peak of the annual festival has always been the look-alike competition, drawing big, gray-bearded men from across the country. Sloppy Joe's co-owner Michael Halpern said the contest would still be held this year.
